t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we will study benzodiazepines from the standpoint of toxicological chemistry. The 1,4-benzodiazepines, that is chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, nitrazepam, oxazepam and phenazepam, are tranquillisers and have toxicological and narcological significance. The aim of the session is to analyse these substances through their hydrolysis products, that is the benzophenones. This method was proposed by B.N. Izotov, I.V. Volkova and others. The plan has three parts: first, isolation and acid hydrolysis; second, detection of benzophenones by TLC; third, photocolorimetric quantification by the Bratton-Marshall reaction.

By the end of the session you should know the following. First, the hydrolysis products: chlordiazepoxide and oxazepam give ACB, diazepam gives MCB, nitrazepam gives ANB, and phenazepam gives BCB. Second, how to distinguish the benzophenone spots on TLC by colour and Rf value, using Table 17. Third, how to compare the cherry-red product formed in the Bratton-Marshall reaction with the standard on the photoelectrocolorimeter. Fourth, how to confirm the result with specific microcrystalloscopic reactions and UV spectrum maxima.

Now the reagents and equipment. For hydrolysis, 10 ml of urine or 2 ml of blood is taken, and 10 ml of concentrated hydrochloric acid is added, 2 ml for blood. The work is done in a flask with a reflux condenser on a water bath. For neutralisation and extraction, the pH is brought to 8-10 with saturated sodium hydroxide solution, then extracted with chloroform twice, 10 ml each time. For TLC, a KSK silica gel plate or Silufol plate is taken; the system is ethyl acetate, methyl alcohol and 25% ammonia in the ratio 85:10:5, and the developing agent is Dragendorff's reagent. For Bratton-Marshall, 10% sodium nitrite, 0.5% ammonium sulphamate and 0.1% naphthylethylenediamine dihydrochloride solutions are needed, along with a photoelectrocolorimeter.

Pay attention to the safety rules. The student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask to the laboratory work. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed after the work. Objects from infectious persons, that is those with tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, arrive in a special container and are marked in the documents. This means that every object must be handled with care.

On the narcological significance of benzodiazepines. In the early 1960s chlordiazepoxide was synthesised, and later diazepam, nitrazepam and oxazepam. The group contains more than 2000 derivatives, of which 12-15 are widely used in medicine. They have sedative, hypnotic and muscle-relaxant effects, and also potentiate the effect of ethyl alcohol, narcotics and hypnotics. With prolonged use they accumulate, and habituation and psychological and physical dependence are observed.

This slide lists the representatives of the 1,4-benzodiazepines and their synonyms. Synonyms of chlordiazepoxide: Elenium, Librium, Napoton. Diazepam: Seduxen, Relanium, Valium. Nitrazepam: Eunoctin, Radedorm, Mogadon. Oxazepam: Tazepam, Nozepam, Serenal. Phenazepam: Phenorelaxan, Elzepam, Tranquizepam. It is important to know the trade names, because in forensic examination materials the drug may appear under exactly these names.

Absorption and metabolism. Benzodiazepines are absorbed rapidly from the gastrointestinal tract; the half-life in blood is on average 1-2 days. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are broken down in the liver by N-demethylation; oxazepam is one of the metabolites of diazepam. Oxazepam binds to glucuronic acid, forming a water-soluble glucuronide, and is excreted in the urine. Nitrazepam is reduced: 7-aminonitrazepam and 7-acetoaminonitrazepam are formed. In the urine only 5% is excreted unchanged, and 95% as metabolites.

Let us go through the diazepam metabolic pathway in sequence. First, diazepam undergoes N-demethylation in the liver. The product of this process is oxazepam. Then oxazepam is bound to glucuronic acid. As a result, a water-soluble glucuronide is formed, which is excreted in the urine. In the same way, chlordiazepoxide is also broken down in the liver by N-demethylation into metabolites.

There are three clinical stages of poisoning. The first is drowsiness and light sleep, the second is superficial coma, that is unconsciousness, and the third is loss of consciousness. Benzodiazepines have psychotropic and neurotoxic effects. If the loss of consciousness lasts more than 12 hours, bronchopneumonia and collapse develop, and liver and kidney function is impaired. In patients lying unconscious, the drug may be found in the stomach even 2-3 days after it was taken.

Remember the key numbers relating to poisoning and half-life. A blood level of 5-20 mg/l leads to poisoning, and 50 mg/l to death. The half-life in blood is on average 1-2 days; oxazepam reaches its maximum concentration in 4 hours. If loss of consciousness lasts more than 12 hours, bronchopneumonia, collapse and impaired liver and kidney function are possible. There are 3 clinical stages.

t: Biological object and basis of isolation
n: Biological object and basis of isolation. The stomach, small intestine, liver and kidney may be taken as the object; isolation is carried out by the method of B.N. Izotov. For hydrolysis, 10 ml of urine or 2 ml of blood is taken as the object. Phenazepam is also isolated from the biological object by the method of B.N. Izotov.

The stages of isolation by Izotov are as follows. The minced object is left for 1 hour with water acidified with HCl, that is at pH=2. The chloroform layer is poured off. The aqueous layer is brought to pH=9-10 and extracted with diethyl ether 3 times. The ether extracts are combined and evaporated, and the dry residue is dissolved in chloroform.

Performing acid hydrolysis in practice. 10 ml of concentrated HCl is added to 10 ml of urine. The mixture is heated in a flask with a reflux condenser for 1 hour on a water bath. After hydrolysis, the pH is brought to 8-10 with saturated NaOH and the mixture is extracted twice with 10 ml of chloroform. The organic layer is separated and evaporated; the residue is analysed by TLC and the substance is identified.

Scheme of acid hydrolysis. The benzodiazepine, that is the substance in urine or blood, is heated with concentrated HCl. Conditions: reflux condenser, 1 hour, water bath. The product is a benzophenone: ACB, MCB, ANB and BCB. When hydrolysis is complete, the pH is brought to 8-10 with NaOH and the mixture is extracted with chloroform. Do not forget that 10 ml is taken for urine and 2 ml for blood, and HCl 10 ml and 2 ml respectively.

The hydrolysis products are benzophenones. Chlordiazepoxide gives ACB, that is 2-amino-5-chlorobenzophenone. Diazepam gives MCB, that is 2-methylamino-5-chlorobenzophenone. Oxazepam also gives ACB. Nitrazepam gives ANB, that is 2-amino-5-nitrobenzophenone. On hydrolysis of phenazepam, BCB is formed. For nitrazepam, along with ANB, DAB, that is 2,5-diaminobenzophenone, is also given. Benzophenones are extracted into chloroform and analysed by TLC.

Analysing benzophenones by TLC. Benzene is used as the chromatographic system. When the plate is taken out of the chamber, yellow spots of varying intensity are seen; the intensity depends on the concentration. Then sodium nitrite, 0.1% hydrochloric acid, 0.5% sulphanilic acid and a solution of naphthol in alkali are sprayed on the plate. After that, the spots are distinguished by colour.

Let us go through the steps of developing the benzophenone spots in sequence. Step one, running in the benzene system. Two, yellow spots appear, with intensity depending on concentration. Three, NaNO2, 0.1% HCl, 0.5% sulphanilic acid and naphthol are sprayed on the plate. As a result, the ACB spot turns red and the ANB spot bright orange. MCB stays yellow, and sometimes the colour disappears.

Remember the colours after spraying, by the table. The ACB spot turns red. The ANB spot is bright orange. The MCB spot stays yellow, and sometimes the colour disappears. Besides the difference in colour, the substances are also identified by their Rf value.

Table 17 gives the Rf and UV spectrum values. For ANB, the nitrazepam product, Rf is 0.17-0.18, UV maxima 238 and 358 nm. For BCB, the phenazepam product, Rf 0.43-0.45, UV 230 and 400. For MCB, the diazepam product, Rf 0.57, UV 238 and 410. For ACB, the chlordiazepoxide product, Rf 0.35-0.37, UV 238 and 390. DAB, formed on hydrolysis of nitrazepam, remains at the start line. On hydrolysis of diazepam, ACB is also given alongside MCB, with an Rf of 0.35-0.37. The values are taken from Table 17 in the toxicological chemistry textbook.

Now testing the benzodiazepines themselves by TLC. A KSK-grade silica gel plate or a Silufol plate is used. System: a mixture of ethyl acetate, methyl alcohol and 25% ammonia solution in the ratio 85:10:5. The spots on the plate are visualised by spraying with Dragendorff's reagent. According to the table, for diazepam the chloroform-acetone 9:1 system and Dragendorff's reagent are used. For oxazepam, chloroform-propyl alcohol-acetone 9:0.4:1; the spot with sodium thiosulphate is yellow or orange. For phenazepam, chloroform-acetone 9:1, an orange spot with Dragendorff's reagent.

Let us sum up the TLC systems. The general system is a mixture of ethyl acetate, methyl alcohol and 25% ammonia, 85:10:5, developed with Dragendorff's reagent. For diazepam, ethyl acetate-ammonia-methanol 26:1.6:3.3 or chloroform-acetone 9:1 is also used. For oxazepam, chloroform-propyl alcohol-acetone 9:0.4:1. For phenazepam, chloroform-acetone 9:1, and also the system benzene-ethanol-diethylamine 9:1:1.

The general colour reaction is carried out with ninhydrin. Ninhydrin is added to the solution and heated on a water bath for 3 minutes. When 5 ml of ethyl alcohol is added, the solution turns blue. Then, when 2 drops of 1% copper sulphate solution are added, a red and then a brown colour forms. Specific results: chlordiazepoxide gives a brown colour, and diazepam gives a yellow-brown product.

Scheme of the ninhydrin reaction. Ninhydrin is added to the benzodiazepine solution. Conditions: water bath, 3 minutes, and 5 ml of alcohol. A blue solution forms. Observation: when 1% CuSO4 is added, the colour is first red, then brown.

Obtaining crystals with precipitating reagents. The chloroform solution is dropped on a microscope slide and the solvent is evaporated; 1 drop of 0.1 N HCl is added to the residue, and after 5-10 minutes the reagent is added. Dragendorff's reagent gives an amorphous precipitate or red crystals. The iron iodide complex after 15 minutes forms dark brown rods. Iodine monochloride, 0.8% alcoholic, gives needle-shaped crystals in 10-15 minutes and prism-shaped crystals after 45-60 minutes. The copper iodide complex in a moist chamber forms dark brown needle-shaped crystals within an hour.

Chlordiazepoxide. A whitish-yellow crystalline powder, readily soluble in water; its main metabolites are N-dimethylchlordiazepoxide and the lactam. With Marquis reagent a yellow mixture forms, with Frohde reagent a flame-red product. UV spectrum: in acid, a maximum at 246 nm and 308 nm; its alkaline solution absorbs light with a maximum at 262 nm. The quantity is determined by spectrophotometric and photoelectrocolorimetric methods.

Kinetic numbers for chlordiazepoxide. After a single dose of 0.015-0.025 g, it is absorbed in 35-45 minutes; the highest blood concentration is seen at 1-8 hours. For the main metabolite, N-dimethylchlordiazepoxide, the highest concentration is reached at 8-24 hours, and the half-life is 6-8 hours. Of the drug, 35-60% is excreted in the urine and 20% in the faeces.

Diazepam. Of the drug, 60-70% is excreted in the urine and 9-10% in the faeces; mainly as metabolites, with a very small amount unchanged. A solution of mercury iodide in potassium iodide gives an amorphous precipitate; in a moist chamber, hexagonal plates and elongated prisms form in 10-15 minutes. The copper thiocyanate complex gives small spheroid crystals; in a moist chamber within 20-30 minutes the crystals merge into aggregates. UV spectrum in acid: 242, 284, 366 nm. The quantity is determined by spectrophotometric and photoelectrocolorimetric methods.

Kinetic numbers for diazepam. After administration, diazepam and its metabolites are detected in blood at 2-6 hours and decrease slowly over 18 hours. The level of N-desmethyldiazepam is at its maximum on days 5-8; the half-life of excretion in the urine is 2-7 days. Of the drug, 60-70% is excreted in the urine and 9-10% in the faeces.

Nitrazepam. For isolation, treatment with saturated oxalic acid, pH=1-2, is carried out 3 times for 1 hour each; then extraction is done with chloroform-ethyl acetate 1:1, in portions of 20, 15 and 15 ml. A 0.1 N iodine solution gives needle-shaped dark brown crystals in 10-15 minutes; a 5% solution of potassium ferricyanide forms prism-shaped crystals. Other benzodiazepine derivatives do not give the reaction with potassium ferricyanide. UV spectrum in ethyl alcohol: 218 and 260 nm; in sulphuric acid: 277 and 340 nm. The quantity is determined by spectrophotometric and photoelectrocolorimetric methods.

Pharmacokinetics of nitrazepam. Nitrazepam was synthesised in 1963; the maximum blood level of 0.005 g is reached after 24 hours. More than 90% of the drug is bound to blood plasma; in 48 hours 23% is excreted. In the urine only 5% is excreted unchanged, and 95% as metabolites.

Oxazepam. A white crystalline powder, practically insoluble in water; readily soluble in ethyl alcohol and chloroform. It is isolated from the biological object by the method of A.F. Fartushny: 3 ml of hydrogen phosphate solution is added to 25 g of the object, and the homogenate is extracted with ethyl ether 3 times, 10 ml each. It is then filtered, and the ether extract is taken for qualitative and quantitative analysis. In plasma it reaches its highest concentration after 4 hours as the glucuronide and disappears from plasma within 48 hours. UV spectrum in acid: 234 and 280 nm; in alkali: 233 and 344 nm. The quantity is determined by spectrophotometric and photoelectrocolorimetric methods.

Phenazepam. A white or pale yellowish crystalline powder; practically insoluble in water and ether; melting point 225-230 °C. It is supplied in tablets of 0.0005-0.001 g and 0.0025 g; it has a strong tranquillising effect. In the Beilstein test, if a crystal on a copper wire is held in a flame, the colourless part of the flame turns green, which indicates organically bound chlorine and bromine. UV spectrum in chloroform: 320 nm; in alcohol: 230 nm. The quantity is determined by spectrophotometric and photoelectrocolorimetric methods.

t: Phenazepam: scheme of the Beilstein test
n: Scheme of the Beilstein test for phenazepam. The organically bound chlorine and bromine in its composition are detected by the Beilstein method. A crystal of phenazepam is placed on a copper wire and held in a flame. Observation: the colourless part of the flame turns green. The product is a copper halide, which is volatile. The test is based on copper forming a volatile salt with a halogen.

Compare the UV maxima for the five substances. Chlordiazepoxide in acid 246 and 308 nm, in alkali 262 nm. Diazepam in acid 242, 284, 366 nm. Nitrazepam in alcohol 218 and 260 nm, in sulphuric acid 277 and 340 nm. Oxazepam in acid 234 and 280 nm, in alkali 233 and 344 nm. Phenazepam in chloroform 320 nm, in alcohol 230 nm.

Quantitative photocolorimetry by the Bratton-Marshall reaction. A 10% solution of sodium nitrite is added to the cooled hydrolysate and left for 3 minutes. Then 0.5 ml of a 0.5% solution of ammonium sulphamate is added and left for a further 3 minutes. Finally, when 0.5 ml of a 0.1% solution of naphthylethylenediamine dihydrochloride is added, a cherry-red solution forms, which is measured on the photoelectrocolorimeter.

Scheme of the Bratton-Marshall reaction. 10% NaNO2 and 0.5% ammonium sulphamate are added to the cooled hydrolysate. After adding sodium nitrite, it is left for 3 minutes; after adding ammonium sulphamate, 0.5 ml, for a further 3 minutes. Then 0.1% naphthylethylenediamine dihydrochloride, 0.5 ml, is added. A cherry-red product forms, which is measured on the photoelectrocolorimeter.

Methods of quantitative analysis. The photocolorimetric method is based on the Bratton-Marshall reaction: a cherry-red product forms. The quantity of benzodiazepine is calculated using a calibration graph. The spectrophotometric method is based on measuring the absorbance at maximum light absorption of alcoholic solutions in the 200-300 nm range.

Interpreting the result. Chlordiazepoxide and oxazepam give the same ACB on hydrolysis, Rf 0.35-0.37, so they cannot be distinguished by this feature alone. To tell them apart, microcrystalloscopic reactions, the UV spectrum and the TLC results for the original substance are needed. Nitrazepam is excreted in urine 95% as metabolites, so it is logical to look for the hydrolysis product ANB.

Review questions. First: how is each of the 1,4-benzodiazepine derivatives isolated from physical evidence? Second: write and explain the hydrolytic cleavage reaction of 1,4-benzodiazepine derivatives. Third: how is nitrazepam and its metabolites detected by TLC? Fourth: how are the colour reaction and the TLC method used in detecting oxazepam carried out?

Conclusion. On hydrolysis benzodiazepines give benzophenones, that is ACB, MCB, ANB, BCB; they are distinguished on TLC by Rf and colour. The substances are confirmed by microcrystalloscopic reactions, the UV spectrum and Bratton-Marshall, photoelectrocolorimetry, and are quantified. The report states the object, the method of isolation, the TLC result, that is Rf and colour, and the quantitative result.
